title: Spousal support
intro: This guide explains what Ontario's Family Law Act and the federal Divorce Act say about support between spouses and former spouses. It describes the law generally; it does not work out whether support is payable in any particular situation or how much.

sections.heading: Who is a “spouse” for support
paragraphs: In the Family Law Act, a “spouse” is either of two persons who “are married to each other”, or who “have together entered into a marriage that is voidable or void, in good faith on the part of a person relying on this clause to assert any right.” (Family Law Act, s. 1 (1))

For support, Part III of the Act goes further. There, “spouse” “in addition includes either of two persons who are not married to each other and have cohabited,” either “continuously for a period of not less than three years” or “in a relationship of some permanence, if they are the parents of a child as set out in section 4 of the Children’s Law Reform Act.” (Family Law Act, s. 29)
The Act defines “cohabit” as “to live together in a conjugal relationship, whether within or outside marriage”. (Family Law Act, s. 1 (1))
In the Divorce Act, “spouse” “includes, in subsection 6(1) and sections 15.1 to 16.96, 21.1, 25.01 and 25.1, a former spouse”. Section 15.2 is the spousal support section. (Divorce Act, s. 2 (1))

sections.heading: The obligation and who can apply under the Family Law Act
paragraphs: The Act says: “Every spouse has an obligation to provide support for himself or herself and for the other spouse, in accordance with need, to the extent that he or she is capable of doing so.” (Family Law Act, s. 30)

“A court may, on application, order a person to provide support for his or her dependants and determine the amount of support.” A “dependant” is “a person to whom another has an obligation to provide support under this Part”. (Family Law Act, ss. 29, 33 (1))

An application for support of a dependant “may be made by the dependant or the dependant’s parent.” Certain government agencies may also apply for the support of a respondent’s spouse or child “if the agency is providing or has provided a benefit” of the kinds the Act lists in respect of the dependant’s support, “or if an application for such a benefit or assistance has been made to the agency by or on behalf of the dependant.” (Family Law Act, s. 33 (2), (3))

Under this Act, “court” means “the Ontario Court of Justice, the Family Court of the Superior Court of Justice or the Superior Court of Justice”. The Act also says “The Limitations Act, 2002 applies to an application made by the dependant’s parent or by an agency referred to in subsection (3) as if it were made by the dependant himself or herself.” (Family Law Act, ss. 1 (1), 33 (2.1))

sections.heading: What a spousal support order should do
paragraphs: Under the Family Law Act, “An order for the support of a spouse should,” (a) “recognize the spouse’s contribution to the relationship and the economic consequences of the relationship for the spouse”; (b) “share the economic burden of child support equitably”; (c) “make fair provision to assist the spouse to become able to contribute to his or her own support”; and (d) “relieve financial hardship, if this has not been done by orders under Parts I (Family Property) and II (Matrimonial Home).” (Family Law Act, s. 33 (8))

sections.heading: What the court considers under the Family Law Act
paragraphs: “In determining the amount and duration, if any, of support for a spouse or parent in relation to need, the court shall consider all the circumstances of the parties”. The listed circumstances include each party’s “current assets and means” and those they are “likely to have in the future”, the dependant’s “capacity to contribute to his or her own support”, the respondent’s “capacity to provide support”, and their “age and physical and mental health”. (Family Law Act, s. 33 (9) (a)-(e))

The list also includes the dependant’s needs, having regard to “the accustomed standard of living while the parties resided together”; the measures available for the dependant to become self-supporting and their time and cost; other legal support obligations; “the desirability of the dependant or respondent remaining at home to care for a child”; and “a contribution by the dependant to the realization of the respondent’s career potential”. (Family Law Act, s. 33 (9) (f)-(j))

Where the dependant is a spouse, the court also considers “the length of time the dependant and respondent cohabited”, “the effect on the spouse’s earning capacity of the responsibilities assumed during cohabitation”, care or education of a child eighteen or over who cannot withdraw from the parents’ charge, “any housekeeping, child care or other domestic service performed by the spouse for the family”, and “the effect on the spouse’s earnings and career development of the responsibility of caring for a child”. (Family Law Act, s. 33 (9) (l))

It also considers “any housekeeping, child care or other domestic service performed by the spouse for the family, as if the spouse were devoting the time spent in performing that service in remunerative employment and were contributing the earnings to the family’s support”. (Family Law Act, s. 33 (9) (l) (v))
The last listed item is “any other legal right of the dependant to support, other than out of public money.” (Family Law Act, s. 33 (9) (m))

On conduct, the Act says “The obligation to provide support for a spouse exists without regard to the conduct of either spouse”. However, in setting the amount the court may consider “a course of conduct that is so unconscionable as to constitute an obvious and gross repudiation of the relationship.” (Family Law Act, s. 33 (10))

sections.heading: Kinds of support orders under the Family Law Act
paragraphs: On a support application the court “may make an interim or final order”. Among other things, it may require “that an amount be paid periodically, whether annually or otherwise and whether for an indefinite or limited period, or until the happening of a specified event”, “that a lump sum be paid or held in trust”, or “that support be paid in respect of any period before the date of the order”. (Family Law Act, s. 34 (1) (a), (b), (f))

The court may also order property transferred to the dependant, require a spouse with life insurance or a pension or benefit plan to name the other spouse or a child as beneficiary, and require “the securing of payment under the order, by a charge on property or otherwise.” (Family Law Act, s. 34 (1) (c), (i), (j), (k))

The Ontario Court of Justice “shall not make an order under clause (1) (b), (c), (i), (j) or (k) except for the provision of necessities or to prevent the dependant from becoming or continuing to be a public charge, and shall not make an order under clause (d).” Clause (d) is an order respecting matrimonial home matters under clause 24 (1) (a), (b), (c), (d) or (e). (Family Law Act, s. 34 (1) (d), (2))

sections.heading: Spousal support under the Divorce Act
paragraphs: Under the Divorce Act, a court “may, on application by either or both spouses, make an order requiring a spouse to secure or pay, or to secure and pay, such lump sum or periodic sums, or such lump sum and periodic sums, as the court thinks reasonable for the support of the other spouse.” The court may also make an interim order while the application is pending. (Divorce Act, s. 15.2 (1), (2))

An order may be “for a definite or indefinite period or until a specified event occurs”, and the court “may impose terms, conditions or restrictions in connection with the order as it thinks fit and just.” (Divorce Act, s. 15.2 (3))

The court “shall take into consideration the condition, means, needs and other circumstances of each spouse, including” (a) “the length of time the spouses cohabited”; (b) “the functions performed by each spouse during cohabitation”; and (c) “any order, agreement or arrangement relating to support of either spouse.” (Divorce Act, s. 15.2 (4))
The court “shall not take into consideration any misconduct of a spouse in relation to the marriage.” (Divorce Act, s. 15.2 (5))

An order “should” (a) “recognize any economic advantages or disadvantages to the spouses arising from the marriage or its breakdown”; (b) “apportion between the spouses any financial consequences arising from the care of any child of the marriage”, over and above child support; (c) “relieve any economic hardship of the spouses arising from the breakdown of the marriage”; and (d) “in so far as practicable, promote the economic self-sufficiency of each spouse within a reasonable period of time.” (Divorce Act, s. 15.2 (6))

Where a court has applications for both child support and spousal support, it “shall give priority to child support in determining the applications.” If that reduces or prevents spousal support, a later reduction or end of child support “constitutes a change of circumstances” for applying for spousal support or a variation. (Divorce Act, s. 15.3 (1), (3))

sections.heading: Agreements about support
paragraphs: Marriage contracts, cohabitation agreements and separation agreements are kinds of “domestic contract”, and each may deal with “support obligations”. A domestic contract is “unenforceable unless made in writing, signed by the parties and witnessed.” (Family Law Act, ss. 51, 52 (1) (b), 53 (1) (b), 54 (b), 55 (1))
“A domestic contract dealing with a matter that is also dealt with in this Act prevails unless this Act provides otherwise.” (Family Law Act, s. 2 (10))

The court “may set aside a provision for support or a waiver of the right to support in a domestic contract” and order support, even if the contract says the support section does not apply, in three situations: if the provision or waiver “results in unconscionable circumstances”; if it involves a dependant “who qualifies for an allowance for support out of public money”; or “if there is default in the payment of support under the contract at the time the application is made.” (Family Law Act, s. 33 (4))
Under the Divorce Act, “any order, agreement or arrangement relating to support of either spouse” is one of the listed factors the court considers. (Divorce Act, s. 15.2 (4) (c))

sections.heading: What the site does not have a source for yet
paragraphs: This site does not yet have a source for the Spousal Support Advisory Guidelines, so this guide does not describe them, what they contain, or how they are used. What this guide covers is limited to the purposes, objectives and factors set out in the Family Law Act and Divorce Act sections above. (Family Law Act, s. 33 (8)-(9); Divorce Act, s. 15.2 (4), (6))
